newsitem.title: USA: Trial of Tyson Foods lobbyist postponed.
newsitem.headline: Trial of Tyson Foods lobbyist postponed.

text.p: The trial of the Washington lobbyist for poultry giant Tyson Foods Inc. was postponed for almost two months Friday after the lead prosecuting attorney was stricken suddenly with appendicitis.

Jack Williams was scheduled to go on trial Friday for allegedly lying to federal agents about his role in helping his company provide favours and gifts to former Secretary of Agriculture Mike Espy. Bob Ray, the prosecting attorny, was stricken with appendicitis Thursday night, the office of Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz said.

Espy resigned from the Clinton cabinet in 1994 amid accusations that he had taken illegal gifts and favours from companies his agency was charged to regulate and has been under investigation by Smaltz for more than two years. The charges against Williams arose from the investigation.

The lengthy probe has resulted in criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns, and convictions of the nation's largest fruit cooperative and close associates of Espy's brother Henry for criminal abuses ranging from money laundering to illegal campaign contributions.

Tyson Foods, the huge Arkansas-based chicken processor whose former chairman has long had close ties with President (Bill) Clinton, has been a focus of the Espy investigation since the start, after it was learned that the firm gave Espy and his girlfriend tickets to a playoff game to the 1993 Super Bowl and a scholarship to Espy's girlfriend.
Williams has been charged with intentionally lying and misleading federal investigators about his knowledge and involvement in the company's overtures to Espy.

Tyson officials have consistently denied any wrongdoing in their relationship with the former agriculture secretary. But legal experts said indictments of the company and even some of its top officials would not be surprising, given the aggressive investigation of the company that Smaltz's team has conducted.

Sources familiar with the investigation said the Williams trial, which is now set to begin March 17, will probably take a week, and should be a fairly straightforward case. They also noted that new information could be revealed in the trial pertaining to Tyson Foods and the company's relationship with former Secretary Espy.
Experts have said the investigation appears to be methodically closing in on Espy. If indicted, Espy would be the first Clinton cabinet member formally charged with criminal wrongdoing.
